question: Six pieces of password advice you have probably followed. Which make an account harder to break into?
answer: The rules that annoy people most protect them least. Forced changes and symbol quotas push people towards predictable tweaks, which cracking software tries first. What works is length, a different password for every site, and a second step at login, because attackers work at scale, from lists of leaked passwords.
move: Judge a security rule by what it costs the attacker, not you.
ask: Which of my accounts would fall if one website I use were breached tomorrow?

items.verdict: People just bump a digit. The US standards body NIST dropped the rule in 2017.

items.note: At least one capital, one digit, one symbol.
items.verdict: Password1! passes. NIST now advises against these rules.

items.note: Four random words in a row.
items.verdict: Each word drawn at random from 7,776 multiplies the guesses needed by 7,776.
Leaked passwords are tried on other sites by the million. One reuse, many doors.

items.note: A code sent to your phone as well.
items.verdict: In Google's tests, even a texted code stopped every automated attack.

items.note: Your mother's maiden name, as a backup.
items.verdict: Often public, or easy to guess: in one Google study, favourite food was often pizza.

reference: NIST Special Publication 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Lifecycle Management, 2017; Google Security Blog, New research: how effective is basic account hygiene at preventing hijacking, May 2019; Bonneau et al., Secrets, Lies, and Account Recovery, WWW 2015
